title: Nothing above a six
author_notes: EC-055 checkpoint-3 coverage: the first Dash/Enter scenario where Dash itself is rated Strong rather than Reasonable or Weak. Compared with bid_training_003 (also low across four suits but reaching 7-8), this hand never rises above a six anywhere, and no suit is long enough to risk the late-establishment pattern from bid_training_005's 7-card Club suit. Independent hand; ratings are authored judgments, not probabilities or guaranteed outcomes.

feedback.title: As safe a zero as this hand gets
feedback.summary: No card in this hand is higher than a six, and no suit is long enough to worry about being established by elimination. Zero is a well-supported plan before trump is even known.
points: Control: there are no Aces, Kings, Queens or Jacks anywhere in this hand — a fact you can check directly against the thirteen cards shown.
Ceiling: the highest card in any suit is a six, so even a generous number of higher cards being played elsewhere leaves little room for one of these to become a winner.
Shape: no suit reaches five cards, so this hand does not carry the long-suit exposure of a 6-7 card holding that can eventually run out of higher cards to hide behind.

This does not guarantee zero: which suit becomes trump and how the round actually plays out are still unknown. The judgment is that this hand supports Dash more confidently than a hand with a 7-8 high card or a long suit would.

feedback.title: Still defensible, just less needed here
feedback.summary: Entering keeps the decision open without committing to a bid. It remains a fair choice, even though this hand gives Dash unusually strong support.
points: Entering does not choose a trick target or trump; that decision is separate and still open either way.
A hand this low and this short in every suit gives little reason to expect a supported four-trick bid later, but entering itself does not claim one.
Choosing to enter here is not wrong — it is simply less supported than Dash by this specific hand's evidence.
